newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.N. agency calls for aid to hungry N.Korean babies.
newsitem.headline: U.N. agency calls for aid to hungry N.Korean babies.

text.p: The World Food Programme (WFP) launched an international appeal on Friday for $95 million to feed hungry babies and toddlers in North Korea, warning famine would strike the impoverished state without urgent supplies.
Catherine Bertini, WFP Executive Director, told a news conference in Seoul the U.N. agency had more than doubled its earlier appeal for $41 million.
The extra money would go to nurseries and kindergartens for children aged under six, who accounted for 2.6 million out of a population of 23 million.
"The additional food aid, almost exclusively, will be directed to children under six, and we will proceed to send food to every nursery and kindergarten throughout the country," she said.
Bertini, who toured North Korea last month, said unless emergency food aid arrived soon "by summer large-scale malnutrition and deaths" would occur.
She said many children in nurseries she visited showed signs of malnutrition. Some had orange-tinted hair, bloated stomachs and limbs.
She showed video footage of children staring blankly.
"We aren't sure how much food the children are receiving in schools right now," Bertini said.
"In one school the teacher said that the children had been fed that day but our nutritionist said there hadn't been any fires that day and food had not been cooked that day."
Bertini said most North Koreans were surviving on 100 grammes (3.5 ounces) of rice or maize per day and supplemented their diets with leaves or roots.
"We visited people in their homes and saw almost no protein source -- no meat, no fish -- and saw empty cupboards and a very limited amount of food," she said.
Bertini said the impoverished Stalinist state needed 2.3 million tonnes of grain to stave off famine.
Pyongyang officials had told her by late March or April the country would run out of food. They asked that limited funds be used to buy maize rather than more expensive rice.
She said the officials told her Pyongyang could scrape together about one million tonnes of food this year. "Using that statistic there will be a shortfall of about 1.3 million tonnes."

Earlier this week a Red Cross official who visited North Korea last week, told reporters in Seoul that kitchens had nothing to offer except for grass and tree bark, children were weak and cattle were being slaughtered to save feed grain.
The South Korean Red Cross on Wednesday sent $1 million worth of food and vegetable seeds, the largest shipment by South Korean religious and civic groups since 1995 floods.
The shipment was scheduled to arrive on Friday afternoon in a port on the west coast of North Korea, a South Korean Red Cross official said.

Bertini said she toured southern areas of North Korea but several Pyongyang officials told her the situation was worse in northern areas where people suffered from internal bleeding caused by eating bark.

Bertini, who leaves Seoul on Saturday after a three-day visit, said she had appealed to South Korean leaders to increase their original pledge of $6 million. The National Unification Ministry said in a statement it would consider the new request.

On Monday, Seoul lifted a ban on private organisations providing rice to Pyongyang. Previously, private groups could only ship non-rice food aid because of fears that rice could be diverted to the military.

The move was widely seen as an effort to lure Pyongyang into four-nation talks with the United States and China aimed at securing a lasting peace to replace an armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
North Korea is insisting on substantial food aid before joining the talks, but Seoul and Washington insist aid can only be discussed during the peace talks.

Separately, South Korea's National Unification Minister Kwon O-kie visiting Japan told a symposium that North Korea could relieve its food shortage "if it only saved one or two percent" from the "billions of dollars spent on the military and on propaganda".

"We hope to help North Korea find a way to catch fish on its own, rather than getting accustomed to taking fish from the outside," Kwon said, adding that South Korea has already given the North $250 million in aid since 1995.
